title: Le, la, les: object pronouns
topic: direct object pronouns in the present; lire and écrire
why: To avoid repeating the same noun, French uses short object pronouns that go before the verb, the opposite of English “I see him”. This lesson covers le, la, l', les, me, te, nous and vous in the present, and adds two useful verbs, lire and écrire.

{"lessons": ["

Him, her, it, them: le, la, les

To avoid repeating a noun, English uses “him”, “her”, “it” or “them” after the verb: “I know her”. French uses a short pronoun too, but it goes before the verb: Je la connais, literally “I her know”. This is the big change to get used to.

— Tu connais Marie ? — Oui, je la connais.— Do you know Marie? — Yes, I know her.
— Tu regardes le film ? — Oui, je le regarde.— Are you watching the movie? — Yes, I'm watching it.
— Tu attends les enfants ? — Oui, je les attends.— Are you waiting for the children? — Yes, I'm waiting for them.
PronounReplacesExample
lea masculine noun: him, itLe bus ? Je le prends.
laa feminine noun: her, itLa clé ? Je la cherche.
l'le or la before a vowel or silent hParis ? Je l'aime beaucoup.
lesa plural noun: themLes livres ? Je les lis.

English “it” has no gender, but French does: you choose le or la according to the noun you're replacing. Le livre → le, la voiture → la. With a vowel, both become l', and with les you hear a liaison: je les‿attends.

Me, you, us

The other persons work the same way, before the verb: me (m'), te (t'), nous, vous.

Tu me cherches ? Je suis là ! Je t'attends devant la gare.Are you looking for me? I'm here! I'm waiting for you in front of the station.
Nos voisins nous invitent samedi. Ils vous invitent aussi ?Our neighbors are inviting us on Saturday. Are they inviting you too?
", "

Where does it go?

The rule is always the same: the pronoun sits right in front of the verb it belongs to. In a negative sentence, ne goes before the pronoun and pas after the verb, so the pronoun stays glued to the verb.

FrenchEnglish
affirmativeJe le connais.I know him.
negativeJe ne le connais pas.I don't know him.
questionTu la connais ?Do you know her?
negative + vowelJe ne l'aime pas.I don't like it.
with an infinitiveJe veux le voir.I want to see him / it.
infinitive + negativeJe ne peux pas les prendre.I can't take them.

With vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, aimer + infinitive, the pronoun goes in front of the infinitive, because that's the verb it belongs to: Tu peux m'attendre ? (Can you wait for me?), Je dois l'appeler (I have to call him / her).

The English trap: verbs without a preposition

Four very common verbs take a preposition in English but none in French. Their object is direct, so they take le / la / les:

FrenchEnglishWith a pronoun
regarder la téléto look at, to watchJe la regarde.
écouter la radioto listen toJe l'écoute.
chercher mes clésto look forJe les cherche.
attendre le busto wait forJe l'attends.

So Je l'attends means “I'm waiting for him” or “I'm waiting for her”, and j'attends pour le bus is wrong. Never add pour after attendre or chercher.

", "

Two new verbs: lire and écrire

Two irregular verbs that go perfectly with object pronouns: you read a book, a message, the newspaper, and you write a letter, a postcard, a text.

lire (to read)écrire (to write)
je / j'lisécris
tulisécris
il / elle / onlitécrit
nouslisonsécrivons
vouslisezécrivez
ils / elleslisentécrivent

The singular forms all sound the same (“lee”, “ay-kree”): the final s and t are silent. The plural reveals a hidden consonant: an s pronounced like z in lisons, lisent, and a v in écrivons, écrivent. Décrire (to describe) is conjugated like écrire.

— Tu lis le journal le matin ? — Oui, je le lis avec mon café.— Do you read the newspaper in the morning? — Yes, I read it with my coffee.
— Elle écrit la carte postale ? — Oui, elle l'écrit pour sa grand-mère.— Is she writing the postcard? — Yes, she's writing it for her grandmother.
Mes enfants ne lisent pas les romans de Zola : ils les trouvent difficiles.My children don't read Zola's novels: they find them difficult.

Note the elision: j'écris, and with a pronoun je l'écris, je ne l'écris pas.

For now, use pronouns for the thing you read or write: Le message ? Je l'écris. Writing to a person uses a different kind of pronoun, which you'll learn later.
